<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:label/>
                    <jats:p>
                      Parent and child sociocultural adaptation is essential to migrant family well‐being, and community‐based mindfulness training may support this process. However, evidence on mindfulness interventions for migrant families remains scarce, particularly those engaging parent and child simultaneously. This study evaluates a parallel parent–child mindfulness intervention targeting sociocultural adaptation, psychological adjustment, and family relationships among Chinese new‐arrival families in Hong Kong. In a randomized controlled trial, 116 parent–child dyads were assigned to an 8‐week mindfulness intervention or routine community services. Outcomes were assessed at baseline, post‐intervention, and 6‐month follow‐up. Compared with controls, the intervention significantly improved parents' sociocultural adaptation, with attenuated effects at follow‐up. It also increased parent life satisfaction and reduced parenting stress at posttest. Child outcomes were largely nonsignificant, except for short‐term improvements in social interaction and life satisfaction at posttest. Indirect effects of the intervention through parent sociocultural adaptation were nonsignificant, with estimates in the hypothesized direction for parent life satisfaction (
                      <jats:italic>B</jats:italic>
                       = 0.94, 95% CI [−0.02, 1.90]) and psychological distress (
                      <jats:italic>B</jats:italic>
                       = −1.42, 95% CI [−2.89, 0.04]). No mediation effects were observed among children. Subgroup analyses indicated that effects on parent adaptation and life satisfaction varied by child sex and family length of residence, with sustained effects observed only among parents of boys and families residing in Hong Kong for less than 2 years. Findings suggest that parallel parent–child mindfulness interventions may support specific aspects of migrant families' adaptation, with more consistent and sustained effects for parents than for children.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Parallel Parent–Child Mindfulness Intervention for Migrant Families' Adaptation: A Randomized Controlled Trial

items.abstract: Continuous mechanical cooling is commonly used to maintain thermal comfort in office environments; however, its influence on human thermophysiological adaptation under sedentary conditions remains poorly understood. This study utilized a randomized parallel-group intervention to determine whether typical office thermal operation influences short-term thermophysiological responsiveness. Over ten weekday intervention exposure sessions distributed across three consecutive calendar weeks, 14 healthy sedentary adults were exposed to either a free-running (FR) or continuously air-conditioned (AC) office environment maintained at a standards-based cooling setpoint. Core body temperature, electrocardiography, skin temperature at the neck and ankles, blood pressure, and perceptual responses were measured during standardized heat-stress tests conducted before and after the intervention. Repeated exposure to the FR environment reduced late-day physiological strain, as indicated by significant attenuation of late-phase core body temperature drift and reduced cumulative afternoon thermal load. FR exposure was also associated with a pronounced reduction in distal skin temperature drift and enhanced late-day parasympathetic cardiac modulation. In contrast, AC exposure did not produce similar adaptive responses and was associated with increased late-day heart rate and reduced parasympathetic activity. Despite these physiological changes, subjective thermal comfort did not improve following FR exposure, and thermal preference remained unchanged in both groups. These findings indicate that routine indoor thermal conditions influence short-term thermophysiological responsiveness in sedentary adults. Continuous air conditioning effectively buffered thermal exposure but was associated with attenuated exposure-driven physiological adaptation. In contrast, modest but repeated thermal variability in free-running offices was sufficient to produce measurable thermophysiological changes within several days.
title: Continuous mechanical cooling attenuates short-term thermophysiological adaptation in office environments: A randomized parallel-group intervention
